summary: Sets out the protocol requirements for SPIRITS, supporting services that start in the telephone network and require interaction with the Internet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a phone call needs help from the Internet. This lists what a protocol must do to allow it.

questions: how do telephone networks request internet services
subtitle: Connecting telephone networks to Internet services with SIP.

tldr.problem: Telephone networks and their Intelligent Network features need to request and interact with Internet services when calls are received. The two domains speak different languages and follow different rules.
tldr.mechanism: SPIRITS defines the protocol requirements for this bridge, using SIP as the signaling base and specifying how telephone detection points (events) map to SIP messages, with different requirements for PSTN, wireless networks, and mixed PSTN/Internet services.
tldr.outcome: This informational document provides the foundation for SPIRITS implementations, establishing a common set of requirements so that telephone switches can trigger Internet services—such as Internet Call Waiting and call forwarding—based on events in the call.

facts.label: Benchmark services
facts.value: Internet Call Waiting, Internet Caller-ID Delivery, Internet Call Forwarding

today: RFC 3298 is an Informational standard and has not been obsoleted. It established the foundation for SPIRITS implementations, though SPIRITS protocol specifications and deployments have evolved since its publication. It remains a reference for understanding the requirements driving PSTN/Internet interworking.

sections.title: Introduction to SPIRITS
sections.content:
SPIRITS stands for Service in the PSTN/IN Requesting InTernet Service. It solves a fundamental problem: telephone switches in the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) use an Intelligent Network (IN) layer to offer advanced services. These services often need to interact with the Internet. For example, Internet Call Waiting notifies a user via email or their computer when a call arrives, and Internet Call Forwarding can redirect calls based on data fetched from an online service.

This document sets out the protocol requirements for SPIRITS based on the architecture in RFC 3136. Unlike PINT (an earlier standard for the other direction, where Internet clients request PSTN services), SPIRITS is initiated by the telephone side. The RFC defines what the SPIRITS protocol must do to enable these hybrid services.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone companies want to add Internet-like features to calls. This part explains what the protocol needs to accomplish and why it's different from earlier work.

sections.title: Architecture and General Requirements
sections.content:
SPIRITS connects three key pieces: the SPIRITS Client (in the telephone Intelligent Network), a SPIRITS Gateway (at the boundary between PSTN and Internet), and a SPIRITS Server (on the Internet side, often co-located with a PINT Server). The two interfaces between them—C (from the telephone side) and B (across the Internet)—must carry the right information securely.

The working group chose Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) as the base protocol. Rather than inventing new message types, SPIRITS carries its specific parameters using SIP's existing extension mechanisms: SDP (Session Description Protocol) and MIME, with a future SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY mechanism for ongoing event notifications. Implementations need not support the earlier PINT standard, but when both are used, they must interwork smoothly.
sections.plainLanguage: A message flows from the telephone network through a gateway to an Internet server. The group decided to use an existing protocol (SIP) instead of building something new, adding telephone-specific information to it.

sections.title: Telephone Detection Points and IN Requirements
sections.content:
Telephone networks use Detection Points (DPs) in the Basic Call State Model (BCSM) to identify events during a call's lifetime. Each DP fires at a specific moment: when a call is authorized, when digits are collected and analyzed, when the called party is busy or does not answer, when the connection is established, when mid-call actions occur, and when the call is terminated.

SPIRITS must map these BCSM detection points (covering IN Capability Set 3 and Wireless IN from ITU-T's IMT 2000 project) to SIP messages. Not all telephone parameters are needed for SPIRITS benchmark services, so the protocol selects the relevant ones for each DP. The SPIRITS Client—typically co-located with the Intelligent Network's Service Control Function—translates telephone events into a text representation suitable for SIP, preserving the original semantics of the telephone parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: A telephone call goes through several moments where something interesting happens—someone picks up, a call gets rejected, the person doesn't answer, the call ends. For each of these, the protocol must carry the information the Internet service needs to decide what to do.

sections.title: Wireless and PINT Considerations
sections.content:
Wireless networks based on circuit switching (CAMEL phase 3 in 3GPP) are treated as PSTN networks for SPIRITS purposes. However, they have unique characteristics: a Home Location Register (HLR) rather than a Service Switching Point (SSP) holds subscriber information, and it generates events like location updates (when a phone moves between coverage areas, or an IMSI attach/detach occurs). These Wireless IN events are communicated to Service Control, which then invokes SPIRITS services using the same mechanism as traditional IN.

When both PINT and SPIRITS are deployed, requirements are shared. For example, both use SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY for event management. The protocol must handle registration (so an IP host can be authenticated before SPIRITS services activate), mixing PSTN event notifications with internet-side responses like accepting, rejecting, or redirecting calls.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile phones create extra complexity: the network needs to know where a user moved, or when they logged in. The protocol must handle these extra events that don't happen on fixed telephone networks.

sections.title: Service Response and Messaging
sections.content:
When an Internet service receives a SPIRITS notification, it must be able to send a response back: accept the incoming call, reject it with a reason code, or redirect it to another number. The SPIRITS protocol defines message types for these actions: ACCEPT, REJECT (with cause), and REDIRECT (with destination). These responses flow from the SPIRITS Server back to the SPIRITS Client and then to the telephone switches' Service Control, which applies the requested action to the call.

For ongoing interaction (such as monitoring call state or requesting that the telephone side arm specific detection points only for this call), the protocol should leverage SIP's SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY mechanism. This allows a SPIRITS Server to ask the SPIRITS Client to watch for future events without requiring a full SIP INVITE for each notification. Both statically configured and dynamically requested detection points are supported.
sections.plainLanguage: After the Internet service learns about a call, it sends back instructions: let the call through, hang it up, or send it somewhere else. The protocol must handle this back-and-forth conversation reliably.

sections.title: Security and Deployment
sections.content:
SPIRITS communication happens across two interfaces with different threat profiles. Interface B (between SPIRITS Gateway and Server) often crosses the public Internet and faces the highest risk of eavesdropping and modification. Interface C (from Service Control to the Gateway) typically stays within a service provider's intranet but still requires protection because it carries sensitive subscriber information. The protocol must support authentication of both endpoints, integrity protection, confidentiality (through encryption), and non-repudiation for charging-related control messages.

The architecture assumes the SPIRITS Client is either co-located with the Intelligent Network Service Control Function or communicates with it securely. This assumption is validated by existing implementations. The security measures chosen should allow compatibility with legacy remote access systems while encouraging migration to stronger authentication mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: A hacker might eavesdrop on messages between the phone network and the Internet to capture sensitive information or impersonate a service. The protocol must have built-in protections so only trusted partners can communicate, the messages can't be altered in transit, and the conversation is encrypted.
